title: Lahore’s old city through routes rather than monuments
summary: Read old Lahore through the spaces between landmarks: approaches, markets, thresholds and the infrastructure that makes an inhabited city work.

body.text: A list of Lahore’s monuments can make the old city seem like a collection of separate destinations. A route changes the emphasis. The interval between a gate, a bathhouse and a mosque becomes part of the story: how people approach, where streets widen, and how a public building meets the neighbourhood outside it. Architecture is no longer only something viewed from the front.

The Walled City of Lahore Authority presents the Royal Trail as a connection between Delhi Gate and Lahore Fort. Its interpretation brings Shahi Hammam, Wazir Khan Mosque, Sonehri Mosque and market spaces into the same account. That is useful not because every building belongs to one reign, but because the route makes different histories legible together. The itinerary is a contemporary interpretive device as well as an account of an older passage.
Thresholds rather than isolated façades

At a city gate, ask what changes between outside and inside: direction, enclosure, the width of passage and the visibility of the next landmark. At a courtyard entrance, compare the compression of the approach with the space beyond. These are observational questions, not a claim that present traffic or paving reproduces Mughal experience. The city has been altered repeatedly, and its current rhythms deserve attention in their own right.

The Authority’s account locates Sonehri Mosque above street level on a raised platform in Kashmiri Bazaar. That relationship is especially revealing. Elevation can distinguish a religious space without removing it from commercial life. Looking at stairs, edges and the street beneath gives a different understanding from looking only at domes. Shops and paths are not simply obstacles to a cleaner photograph; they help explain the setting in which the monument is encountered.
The route below the paving

AKDN’s 2022 project report describes work along a 383-metre stretch from Delhi Gate to Chowk Purani Kotwali. The programme included utilities, sewerage, paving and street furniture alongside architectural conservation. Its stated sequence placed safety and drainage before decorative finishing. These details make an important distinction: improving the appearance of a street and sustaining a usable neighbourhood are related, but they are not the same task.

The same report describes community involvement and training within the rehabilitation programme. Those are project-reported activities, not proof that every resident experienced the work identically. A fuller social history would add residents’ accounts, including disagreements and changing livelihoods. A heritage walk should leave room for such voices rather than turning inhabited lanes into a theatrical background.

Read the trail in both directions. Returning along an approach can reveal a doorway or change in scale that the outward journey concealed. Leave entrances clear, ask before photographing people, and distinguish a public route from permission to enter a private building. Lahore’s old city becomes richer when the connections between its landmarks receive as much attention as the landmarks themselves.

title: Chiniot and the relationship between craft and patronage
summary: Chiniot’s Shahi Masjid and Gulzar Mahal reveal different relationships between commissioning, skilled work and the survival of makers’ names.

body.text: Patronage is often reduced to a name on a building: the ruler, merchant or official who paid for it. Chiniot offers a more demanding question. How did a commission become a structure through the work of designers, masons, carvers and painters? Two official inventory entries—the Shahi Masjid and Gulzar Mahal—preserve very different kinds of evidence for answering it.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums describes Shahi Masjid as a brick mosque with three domes and a courtyard ablution tank. Stone appears selectively at entrances and in the bases of architectural supports. The record also notes traces of painted floral and geometric ornament inside the prayer chamber. Rather than treating the mosque as an undifferentiated decorative object, these details identify distinct tasks: laying masonry, shaping durable thresholds and preparing painted surfaces.
A commission divided among skills

Gulzar Mahal’s inventory is unusually specific about people. It credits architect Syed Hassan Shah and names Rahim Bakhsh and Elahi Bakhsh for woodcarving, Ahmad Din for brickwork, Niaz Ahmad Jalandari for stucco, and Jan Muhammad for frescoes. These attributions are reported by the catalogue; they should not be mistaken for independently examined contracts. Nevertheless, they offer a valuable starting point for restoring makers to an account usually dominated by a mansion’s owner.

The distinction between those trades matters. A carved ceiling must be supported and fitted; painted ornament depends on a prepared ground; stucco negotiates the junction between structure and surface. The finished room conceals much of this sequencing. Looking for joints, changes of material and the edges of panels helps reveal collaboration without inventing the words or working conditions of the people involved.

The record places the mansion’s completion in 1935 and connects its commission with Sheikh Omar, a businessman returning to Chiniot. Its account also contains family stories and dramatic explanations for abandonment. Those narratives need a different evidential footing from the surviving fabric. They are not necessary to appreciate the documented range of skills, and they should not become the main explanation of the building’s significance.
Survival changes the commission

The catalogue describes the loss of upper levels and later conservation associated with conversion to a research centre and library. That history complicates any photograph presented as the original whole. What survives is both a record of ambitious making and a record of subsequent removal, repair and reuse. A description should identify which of those histories it is discussing.

Comparing the mosque and mansion does not establish an unbroken workshop genealogy. Similar materials can be used centuries apart by different networks of workers. What the comparison does reveal is how commissioning becomes visible at several scales: the organisation of a courtyard, the selection of a stone threshold, or the fitting of an ornamental panel. Chiniot’s architectural history is strongest when it makes room for those different scales—and for the named and unnamed people whose labour connected them.

title: Bahawalpur’s princely building programme
summary: Bahawalpur’s princely architecture connects palace display, religious patronage and public institutions, rather than a single style or building campaign.

body.text: Bahawalpur’s princely building history is not a sequence of interchangeable palaces. It includes spaces for residence, ceremony, worship, education and administration. Reading these together changes the question from which building looks most impressive to how a ruling household presented authority and supported institutions across a city.

Noor Mahal is a useful starting point because its dates require care. The federal inventory associates the palace with 1872. The district government’s fuller account identifies that as the foundation year and gives 1875 for completion. These statements need not be contradictory if construction is understood as a process. A single date beneath a photograph can conceal design, building, occupation and later additions.
Display and adaptation

The district account describes classical elements in Noor Mahal’s columns, pediments and balustrades alongside domed forms. It also records a mosque added in 1906. The building therefore resists a simple choice between imported and local architecture. Its surfaces and spaces were assembled for a particular princely setting, and later work extended that setting. Architectural comparison is most useful when it identifies an element precisely instead of assigning the entire palace to one cultural category.

The account of Noor Mahal’s subsequent institutional custody adds another layer. A former princely building can retain its name while its users, access arrangements and responsibilities change. This is why an architectural history should not double as a promise of current opening hours. Nor should the familiar story of a reluctant royal resident be used as an established explanation of how the whole palace functioned.
Beyond the palace gate

Jame Masjid Al-Sadiq provides a different kind of evidence. Its inventory attributes a renovation in 1935 to Sir Sadiq Muhammad Khan Abbasi. The same entry contains an inconsistent broad chronology field, so it cannot establish an early-medieval date for the present building. The defensible point here is narrower: princely patronage included the renewal of a religious institution, not only the construction of residences.

The district’s city history also records educational and civic milestones, including Sadiq Egerton College in 1886 and Jamia Abbasia in 1925. These institutions widen the frame beyond palace façades. A building programme can shape a city through teaching, administration and service as well as courtly display. The survival of an institution and the survival of its earliest fabric remain separate questions, requiring building-specific investigation.
A programme, not one blueprint

It is tempting to arrange these places as a smooth story of benevolent progress. A better account leaves room for different patrons, political relationships and users, and asks who could enter each space. Ceremony, education and congregational worship organise access differently. Comparing their entrances and public edges can make those distinctions tangible without pretending that architecture alone reveals every social relationship.

Bahawalpur’s princely legacy is therefore best read as a changing network. Noor Mahal gives one view of display; Al-Sadiq another of religious renewal; educational institutions another of public ambition. None can stand for the entire city, but together they make its architectural history more substantial than a gallery of royal interiors.

title: The Cholistan fort network and its uneven survival
summary: Derawar is only one part of Cholistan’s fort landscape. Smaller and damaged structures change how the network’s history should be understood.

body.text: Derawar’s recognisable outline can overshadow the other forts of Cholistan. Yet a network cannot be understood through its most photogenic member alone. Smaller enclosures, damaged walls and partly lost plans are evidence too. They help test whether the forts shared functions, how their forms differed, and why some survive more visibly than others.

Pakistan’s Tentative List submission, published by UNESCO in 2016, proposes Derawar and the desert forts as a related landscape. Tentative listing is not World Heritage inscription. The submission links the structures with movement, water and political control, while acknowledging that the network’s precise extent and character need further exploration. This is an argument for research and comparison, not a licence to draw a fully proven route between every fort.
Different buildings within the landscape

The federal inventory’s Marot entry, drawing on Mohammad Rafique Mughal’s work, describes a rectangular enclosure and surviving corner bastions. It also reports that much of the layout had disappeared by the documented assessment. That description is a historical condition record, not a fresh survey. Its value lies partly in the features it recorded before further change, and partly in the questions it leaves for present documentation.

Mirgarh’s entry gives a different picture: a compact square fort, an outer earthen rampart and wells inside and outside the enclosure. The catalogue associates its construction with Nur Muhammad Khan at the end of the eighteenth century. Even without accepting every measurement as a current field observation, the contrast with Marot is useful. Size, enclosure and water provision need to be compared individually rather than assumed from Derawar’s form.
Visibility is not importance

A tall standing wall offers a strong photograph. A low mound may preserve a more complex sequence underground. The difference is one of visibility, not automatically one of historical value. A damaged fort can still help establish building phases, access arrangements or the relationship between an enclosure and nearby water infrastructure. Removing loose material to make it more legible would destroy precisely the evidence needed to answer those questions.

The Tentative List account presents continued occupation as one reason for Derawar’s comparatively strong survival. That explanation should not be generalised to every site. Different materials, repair histories and local circumstances can produce very different results. Nor should the apparent absence of a wall on a visitor photograph be treated as proof that a feature never existed.
Reading the network responsibly

An effective comparison begins with modest, consistent observations: the shape of the enclosure, the position of entrances, evidence for rebuilding and the relationship to documented wells. It then distinguishes measured features from proposed connections. The resulting map will have gaps, but those gaps are more useful than an elegant line that claims certainty it does not possess.

Cholistan’s forts belong together without becoming identical. Derawar can introduce the landscape; it cannot replace it. Bringing Marot, Mirgarh and other recorded structures into the account shifts attention from a single monumental silhouette to the uneven survival of an entire historical system.

title: Multan’s many building histories
summary: Multan’s monumental tomb, tiled shrine and municipal clock tower reveal histories that cannot be reduced to a single architectural identity.

body.text: Multan is frequently introduced through its shrines, but even its religious architecture does not follow one formula. A comparison between Shah Rukn-i-Alam and Shah Yusuf Gardezi immediately reveals different approaches to mass, surface and enclosure. Adding the municipal clock tower makes the city’s changing institutional history visible as well. These are not three illustrations of one timeless style.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums records Shah Rukn-i-Alam’s tomb as an octagonal structure articulated with buttresses, brickwork, tile and timber. The arrangement directs attention to the relationship between construction and ornament. Horizontal bands do more than colour a surface: they help a viewer read the mass in stages. The building’s scale and repeated angles create a very different encounter from a small rectangular shrine.
Two ways of making a sacred exterior

The official catalogue describes Shah Yusuf Gardezi’s tomb as a single-storey, flat-roofed rectangle with relatively unbroken walls and extensive coloured tile facing. Here, the surface becomes particularly important. A comparison should not rank one structure above the other by size. It should ask how each establishes an exterior, marks an entrance and distinguishes a sacred interior from its surroundings.

Neither description permits every visible tile to be dated to the first construction. Repairs, replacements and later embellishment require their own evidence. A saint’s lifetime, the foundation of a shrine and the age of its present fabric are different historical questions. Keeping them separate makes a building history more informative, not less respectful of religious memory.
Municipal authority enters the picture

Multan’s Ghanta Ghar introduces another institutional language. The inventory dates the municipal complex to 1884–88 and places it beside the old fort area. It records the names Ripon Hall and Northbrook Tower, followed by Jinnah Hall after independence. These names are evidence of changing public commemoration as well as a way of identifying the building.

A clock tower makes time visible in the street. A municipal hall places administration within an architectural setting. Their conjunction invites a different reading from that of a tomb: not only what the façade resembles, but how government represented itself to people moving through the city. This is interpretation of the building type, not proof of how every resident understood it.

The catalogue also recounts reuse proposals and periods of disuse, but those observations belong to the dates of its sources. They should not be turned into an assertion about today’s museum provision. A historic building can remain an important landmark even while its institutional programme changes or remains unsettled.
A city with several architectural histories

The three buildings offer a compact way to resist a single-style portrait of Multan. Compare a buttressed octagon, a tile-clad rectangle and a civic tower. Then compare the kinds of records each needs: conservation evidence, religious histories, municipal archives and accounts from users. The city becomes more legible when those sources are allowed to differ. Its architectural richness lies in relationships between such histories, not in making them all tell the same story.

title: Rawalpindi’s merchant neighbourhoods and transport links
summary: Rawalpindi’s domestic courtyards and transport infrastructure suggest an urban history larger than either a merchant mansion or a railway landmark alone.

body.text: A mansion and a railway station preserve different scales of urban life. One organises entry into a household; the other gathers movement across a wider territory. Rawalpindi’s history becomes more interesting when these scales are considered together, without assuming that every grand house was financed by railway commerce or that a transport line explains the whole city.

The federal inventory describes Sujan Singh’s haveli through its entrance sequence: an ornate door, entrance rooms, a portico and an interior courtyard. Rooms and halls occupy different sides, while narrow stairs connect levels. These details suggest a way to read domestic architecture through controlled movement. The significance of the house is not exhausted by the richness of its front elevation.
The household within a changing neighbourhood

The entry draws on a 2014 condition assessment and describes a late-nineteenth-century building once associated with gardens. That historical setting matters. A house’s original relationship to open ground may differ from the dense urban context encountered later. Changes around a building can alter light, views and approaches without changing its name. A present-day street photograph cannot, on its own, reconstruct the earlier property boundary.

Such a mansion is also an uneven source. It makes wealth and spatial organisation visible more readily than it makes domestic labour visible. Kitchens, stairs and service approaches may help formulate questions, but they cannot supply unnamed workers’ biographies. Reading a merchant neighbourhood responsibly means seeking commercial records and family or community histories alongside architectural description.

The Urban Unit’s regional tourism report treats Rawalpindi Railway Station as a late-nineteenth-century transport landmark linking the city with a larger network. That connection provides context, not a complete explanation of urban change. To demonstrate how a particular business depended on rail, one would need records of goods, firms or journeys rather than the simple presence of both a station and a prosperous house.
A district is not a single town

Khem Singh Bedi’s haveli at Kallar Syedan offers a useful regional comparison. Its catalogue records courtyards, verandas, projecting windows and painted surfaces. But it is not a second stop in Rawalpindi’s old-city street system merely because an older inventory groups it under Rawalpindi District. Administrative labels can conceal considerable geographical distance and different settlement histories.

Comparing the two houses can reveal different arrangements of rooms and display. It should not collapse their patrons, communities or settings into a generic description of a Sikh mansion. Nor should an older statement that paintings were well preserved be treated as a current condition report or permission to enter.

Rawalpindi’s built history is therefore best approached as a set of relationships to investigate: house and street, neighbourhood and market, city and transport network. Begin with what each source actually records, then ask how the pieces connect. The result is less tidy than a single story of railway-driven prosperity, but much closer to the complexity of an inhabited city.

title: The Salt Range as a corridor of different periods
summary: The Salt Range’s temples reward comparison across form and time. A corridor is a framework for questions, not proof that every site belongs to one phase.

body.text: A regional map can make the Salt Range’s temples look like a unified group. Their proximity invites comparison, but it does not make them contemporary or architecturally identical. The most useful question is how a regional tradition accommodated different forms over time—and how confidently those differences can be dated.

In his 1996 preliminary study for Penn Museum, architectural historian Michael W. Meister examined temples in the Salt Range and along the Indus. He argued against treating the whole group simply as an extension of Kashmiri architecture. His discussion of Malot was particularly important: a building with conspicuous affinities to Kashmir need not define every other temple in the region.
Compare a detail, not only a silhouette

Meister’s analysis draws attention to small representations of shrines on temple walls. These are architecture depicting architecture. Their towers, niches and roof forms can be compared with the larger structures that carry them. A small carved feature may therefore preserve evidence for architectural choices that a damaged superstructure no longer reveals directly.

This is a useful lesson for looking. Begin with a bounded feature—a doorway, a cornice or a shrine model—and describe its shape before assigning it a period. A curved outline and a stepped outline are not interchangeable. Equally, a resemblance is the beginning of an argument, not proof that the same workshop, patron or community produced both objects.

The official Malot inventory describes recessed faces, columns and trefoil arches, and reconstructs the lost roof cautiously. Its historical attribution differs from the framework developed in Meister’s later discussion. Presenting both sources as though they supplied one exact date would erase a real interpretive problem. The visible fabric, an older catalogue and a scholarly stylistic sequence are different kinds of evidence.
The limits of a corridor

A corridor is a helpful way to think about connections, but it should not become a conveyor belt carrying a single style in one direction. Materials, patrons and builders can move through networks while producing locally distinctive buildings. Similarities may indicate contact, shared conventions or later imitation; distinguishing those possibilities requires more than the line joining two map markers.

Meister explicitly presented much of his chronology as a developing argument that further archaeological work could refine. That qualification belongs in the story. A date based mainly on architectural comparison has a different evidential status from an inscription or a securely excavated deposit. Neither should be silently substituted for the other.

The Salt Range rewards a layered itinerary of attention rather than a race through monuments. Notice what survives, what is reconstructed in a drawing and what a source only proposes. Keep the temple’s setting in view without treating nearby remains as automatically part of the same foundation. Such distinctions do not diminish the landscape’s coherence. They allow its coherence to emerge from specific relationships rather than from a single broad label imposed in advance.

title: Gujranwala before and after the Sikh court
summary: Gujranwala’s haveli, dynastic memorial and Jain shrine tell related but distinct stories of authority, commemoration and urban memory.

body.text: Gujranwala is closely associated with Ranjit Singh, but the city’s surviving architecture should not be reduced to an illustrated royal biography. A residence, a memorial to his father and a later Jain shrine preserve different relationships between a community and its past. Reading them separately also prevents similar architectural forms from producing mistaken identities.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums catalogues a haveli as Ranjit Singh’s birthplace. Its description records a formal entrance front, a large reception space and a sequence of courtyards. Those features help explain how a substantial household organised approach and access. The attribution of a particular room as a birthplace is a narrower commemorative claim, not something the room’s architecture can independently prove.
Residence and remembrance

A residence accommodates changing daily uses. A memorial selects a life or event for public remembrance. Mahan Singh’s samadhi belongs to the second category. The official entry describes an octagonal structure with a domed upper chamber and painted interiors, and connects its commission with Ranjit Singh’s patronage. The building therefore tells us about remembrance after Mahan Singh’s life, not simply about the period in which he governed.

The source’s chronological details are not entirely consistent, so an exact death date is not necessary to the present comparison. More securely, its architectural description identifies a symmetrical composition, projecting eaves and arched openings. These features offer a basis for comparison with other buildings without requiring a claim that one community exclusively owned a visual language.

The record also contains condition observations inherited from earlier documentation. They explain why a surviving fragment of painting matters, but they are not a current survey. A damaged interior is not permission to enter, touch or retrieve loose material. The relationship between a memorial and neighbouring occupation deserves documentation rather than a picturesque description of neglect.
A Jain shrine is not another royal samadhi

Atmaramji Shrine commemorates the Jain teacher Acharya Vijayanand Suri. The catalogue places its construction around the turn of the twentieth century and notes formal similarities with nearby memorial architecture. It also cautions against an identification with Ranjit Singh’s grandfather that arose from those similarities. Here, naming is not a minor matter: a wrong label can erase the community and individual actually commemorated.

The comparison provides a practical lesson. An octagonal chamber or dome can travel across different religious and patronage settings. Form alone cannot establish dedication. Inscriptions, institutional histories and community knowledge need to be read alongside architectural resemblance. Shared craftsmanship and shared identity are not equivalent claims.

Together, these three places make a more complex Gujranwala visible. The haveli frames domestic authority; Mahan Singh’s samadhi frames dynastic memory; Atmaramji Shrine frames a Jain community’s commemoration. Their proximity creates opportunities for comparison, not reasons to merge their stories. The city’s heritage becomes clearer when the distinctions are maintained and the connections are explained with equal care.

title: Bhera and the memory of a river town
summary: Bhera’s river setting, altered gates and repeatedly rebuilt mosque show why a town’s age cannot be read from a single origin story.

body.text: Bhera’s history is often compressed into a claim about exceptional antiquity. A more revealing starting point is its position beside the Jhelum and the different kinds of movement associated with it. Rivers, roads, gates and markets do not all preserve the same chronology. Their relationship can explain a town without requiring every visible building to belong to its earliest remembered phase.

The federal inventory places Bhera on the river’s left bank and describes routes associated with salt traffic branching towards Lahore and Multan. It also repeats an identification with the capital of Sophytus, a contemporary of Alexander. The first is a geographical and route-history proposition; the second is a much more demanding ancient identification. It should not be treated as established merely because it appears beside a modern place name in a catalogue.
Gates that remember rebuilding

The same record describes an eight-gated walled town associated with Sher Shah Suri and notes substantial nineteenth-century reconstruction of gateways. That combination matters. A gate can preserve the memory and location of an older approach while containing later fabric. Calling it old does not answer which part is old, when it was repaired or how its surrounding street changed.

Rather than seeking a completely untouched town, look for differences between the passage, its façade and the buildings that now meet it. A rebuilt arch may retain a route even where an earlier wall has disappeared. Conversely, an impressive façade does not prove the survival of a complete defensive system. These are questions to investigate through plans and dated photographs, not conclusions available from appearance alone.
A mosque with more than one date

Jame Masjid’s inventory associates its foundation with Sher Shah and reports a 1541 date on the entrance. It separately records rebuilding under Qazi Ahmed-ud-din Bugvi in 1858 and repair under Qazi Zahoor Ahmed Bugvi in 1926. The account also preserves the name of mason Muhammad Asif. These details turn a simple foundation story into a history of continued investment and skilled work.

The present building therefore cannot be described responsibly as an unchanged sixteenth-century object. Its domes, halls, painted plaster and institutional spaces need to be understood through their individual phases. The association with an early patron remains meaningful, but it is not a date stamp applied to every wall. Later rebuilding is part of the monument’s significance rather than an embarrassment to be omitted.

Bhera’s river-town identity emerges from this layering. Routes can persist while gateways change; a religious institution can endure through major reconstruction; an ancient name can remain debated while later history is well documented. These are not competing versions from which one must choose the most romantic. They describe different kinds of continuity. Keeping them distinct allows the town’s memory to remain expansive without making its evidence appear more certain than it is.

title: Faisalabad: a planned town and its later city
summary: Faisalabad’s planned centre is only one chapter in a regional history that includes Sandal Bar, canal settlement, commerce and textile production.

body.text: Faisalabad’s clock tower and eight bazaars make a strong image of a planned city. Yet a plan is a beginning of inquiry, not a complete urban history. It shows how a centre was organised, but it does not explain every later business, journey or neighbourhood. Nor does the creation of a colonial town imply that its wider landscape previously lacked people or history.

The district government dates the clock tower’s construction to 1903–05 and describes the eight-bazaar arrangement around it. The monument provides a common point of reference for several approaches. That is different from treating it as an isolated object in a square: its urban significance depends on the streets that bring people towards it and distribute them away again.
A plan encountered at street level

A diagram makes a radial arrangement look immediate and orderly. Walking through it is a different experience. A person sees one approach, a partial view of the tower and the changing frontage of a particular market. The distinction between a bird’s-eye plan and a ground-level journey helps explain why a designed centre can acquire many local identities without losing its overall geometry.

The district account also identifies Kaiseri Gate and the Gumti with 1897, and places the gate at the entrance to Rail Bazaar. These smaller structures widen the reading beyond the tower. Commemorative architecture and commercial approaches can overlap, while later changes in use or symbolism alter what a place means. The presence of a colonial-era monument does not freeze the surrounding market in its original social setting.
The region before and beyond Lyallpur

Lyallpur Museum’s recorded gallery structure offers an important counterweight to a tower-centred account. Its subjects include Sandal Bar, regional archaeology, the Chenab Colony, Lyallpur and textiles. These categories connect a planned urban centre to a wider environmental, settlement and productive history. The museum’s use of the older city name also makes naming itself part of the historical conversation.

The gallery list is not a substitute for inspecting individual objects and their labels. It does, however, show why the city cannot be explained solely through a colonial plan. A canal-colony history asks about land and settlement; a textile history asks about production and labour; an archaeological history reaches beyond the chronology of the modern centre. Each requires different sources and raises different questions about change.
A city outgrows its founding image

The useful contrast is not between a perfect old plan and a disorderly later city. It is between the intentions recorded in a plan and the many purposes that people subsequently bring to streets and buildings. A market is made through use as well as design. Its history includes adaptation, subdivision and changing forms of work.

Faisalabad’s planned centre remains an excellent point of orientation. It becomes a richer heritage subject when the tower is read together with its bazaars and with the regional histories presented by the museum. The result is a city with a designed centre, not a city whose entire identity can be reduced to a design.
